summary: This standards-track document describes RADIUS, a protocol that carries authentication, authorization and configuration information between a network access server and a shared authentication server. It was replaced by RFC 2865.

plainLanguage.summary: RADIUS lets one server hold the user database for many dial-in servers. The dial-in server sends the user's name and a scrambled password to the RADIUS server, which checks them and sends back either a refusal, a request for more information, or a list of connection settings to apply.

questions: what is a nas in radius
subtitle: How a dial-in server asks a shared server whether a user may connect, and what service to give them.

tldr.problem: An organisation with many dial-in lines and modems needs one place to check user names and passwords and to decide what each user gets, rather than keeping that information on every access server.
tldr.mechanism: RADIUS is a client/server protocol. The Network Access Server sends an Access-Request over UDP to port 1812 with the user's name and a hidden password, and the server replies with Access-Accept, Access-Reject or Access-Challenge, optionally carrying the settings the client should apply.
tldr.outcome: One shared server can authenticate and configure users for many access servers, and new attributes can be added without changing the protocol. The document has been replaced by RFC 2865.

today: RFC 2138 was a Proposed Standard published in April 1997. It has been obsoleted by RFC 2865, which is the current RADIUS specification.

sections.title: What RADIUS Is For
sections.content:
Managing dispersed serial line and modem pools for large numbers of users can create the need for significant administrative support. Since modem pools are by definition a link to the outside world, they require careful attention to security, authorization and accounting. This can be best achieved by managing a single database of users, which allows for authentication, verifying user name and password, as well as configuration information detailing the type of service to deliver to the user, for example SLIP, PPP, telnet or rlogin.

The key features of RADIUS are a client/server model and network security. A Network Access Server operates as a client of RADIUS: the client is responsible for passing user information to designated RADIUS servers, and then acting on the response which is returned. The RADIUS servers are responsible for receiving user connection requests, authenticating the user, and then returning all configuration information necessary for the client to deliver service to the user. A RADIUS server can also act as a proxy client to other RADIUS servers or to other kinds of authentication servers.

Transactions between the client and the RADIUS server are authenticated through the use of a shared secret, which is never sent over the network. In addition, any user passwords are sent encrypted between the client and the RADIUS server, to eliminate the possibility that someone snooping on an unsecure network could determine a user's password. The RADIUS server can support a variety of methods to authenticate a user: when it is provided with the user name and original password, it can support PPP PAP or CHAP, UNIX login, and other authentication mechanisms. All transactions are comprised of variable length Attribute-Length-Value triples, so new attribute values can be added without disturbing existing implementations of the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: One server holds the user list, and the machines that actually accept the connections ask it. The two share a secret that never crosses the network, and the password itself is scrambled on the way.

sections.title: The Exchange Between the NAS and the Server
sections.content:
When a client is configured to use RADIUS, any user of the client presents authentication information to the client, perhaps with a customizable login prompt, or through a link framing protocol such as PPP. Once the client has obtained such information, it creates an Access-Request containing attributes such as the user's name, the user's password, the ID of the client and the Port ID which the user is accessing. When a password is present it is hidden using a method based on the RSA Message Digest Algorithm MD5. The Access-Request is submitted to the RADIUS server via the network; if no response is returned within a length of time the request is re-sent a number of times, and the client can also forward requests to an alternate server if the primary is down or unreachable.

Once the RADIUS server receives the request, it validates the sending client. A request from a client for which the server does not have a shared secret should be silently discarded. If the client is valid, the server consults a database of users to find the user whose name matches the request. The user entry contains a list of requirements which must be met to allow access, always including verification of the password, but also possibly the client or port to which the user is allowed access.

If any condition is not met, the server sends an Access-Reject, and MAY include a text message which MAY be displayed by the client to the user. No other attributes are permitted in an Access-Reject. If all conditions are met and the server wishes to issue a challenge, it sends an Access-Challenge, which MAY include a text message to display and MAY include a State attribute. On receiving an Access-Challenge the client displays the message, prompts the user for a response, and re-submits its original Access-Request with a new request ID, with the User-Password attribute replaced by the encrypted response and the State attribute from the challenge. If all conditions are met, the list of configuration values for the user are placed into an Access-Accept response. These include the type of service, for example SLIP, PPP or Login User, and all necessary values to deliver the desired service: for SLIP and PPP this may include values such as IP address, subnet mask, MTU, desired compression and desired packet filter identifiers, and for character mode users it may include the desired protocol and host.
sections.plainLanguage: The access server sends what it knows, the RADIUS server checks it, and the reply is one of four things: accept with settings, reject, ask a question and wait for the answer, or ask again with another question.

sections.title: The Packet Format and the Packet Types
sections.content:
Exactly one RADIUS packet is encapsulated in the UDP data field, where the UDP destination port field indicates 1812. When a reply is generated, the source and destination ports are reversed. The memo notes that there has been some confusion in the assignment of port numbers: the early deployment of RADIUS used the erroneously chosen port number 1645, which conflicts with the datametrics service, while the officially assigned port is 1812.

The packet begins with a Code field of one octet that identifies the type of packet, an Identifier field of one octet that aids in matching requests and replies, and a Length field of two octets that indicates the length of the packet including the Code, Identifier, Length, Authenticator and Attribute fields. Octets outside the range of the Length field should be treated as padding and ignored, and if the packet is shorter than the Length field indicates it should be silently discarded. The minimum length is 20 and the maximum length is 4096.

The Authenticator field is sixteen octets, with the most significant octet transmitted first. It is used to authenticate the reply from the RADIUS server and in the password hiding algorithm. In an Access-Request the value is a 16 octet random number called the Request Authenticator, which SHOULD be unpredictable and unique over the lifetime of a secret, since repetition of a request value in conjunction with the same secret would permit an attacker to reply with a previously intercepted response. In Access-Accept, Access-Reject and Access-Challenge packets the value is called the Response Authenticator and contains a one-way MD5 hash over the RADIUS packet together with the shared secret, that is, MD5 of the Code, Identifier, Length, Request Authenticator and response Attributes followed by the Secret.

The RADIUS codes are 1 Access-Request, 2 Access-Accept, 3 Access-Reject, 4 Accounting-Request, 5 Accounting-Response, 11 Access-Challenge, 12 Status-Server and 13 Status-Client, with 255 reserved. An implementation wishing to authenticate a user MUST transmit a packet with the Code field set to 1. An Access-Request MUST contain a User-Name attribute, MUST contain either a User-Password or a CHAP-Password attribute, and SHOULD contain either a NAS-IP-Address or a NAS-Identifier attribute, as well as a NAS-Port or NAS-Port-Type attribute where ports are distinguished.
sections.plainLanguage: Every RADIUS packet has the same four-part header: a one-byte type, a one-byte number to match the reply, a two-byte length, and a 16-byte value used to check the reply and to hide the password.

sections.title: Attributes
sections.content:
Attributes are the variable length parts that carry the information. Many attributes may have multiple instances, in which case the order of attributes of the same type SHOULD be preserved, while the order of attributes of different types is not required to be preserved. The User-Name attribute carries the user's name and identifies the user in the server's database, and the User-Password attribute carries the user's password. When a password is present it is hidden: the NAS and the RADIUS server share a secret, the shared secret followed by the Request Authenticator is put through a one-way MD5 hash to create a 16 octet digest value which is xored with the password entered by the user, and the xored result is placed in the User-Password attribute.

The CHAP-Password attribute carries the response to a CHAP challenge. For CHAP, the NAS generates a random challenge, preferably 16 octets, and sends it to the user, who returns a CHAP response along with a CHAP ID and CHAP username. The RADIUS server looks up the password based on the User-Name, encrypts the challenge using MD5 over the CHAP ID octet, that password and the CHAP challenge, and compares the result to the CHAP-Password. If they match the server sends Access-Accept, otherwise Access-Reject. If the password is not available in cleartext to the RADIUS server then the server MUST send an Access-Reject.

Several attributes describe the access server itself, such as NAS-IP-Address, NAS-Port, NAS-Identifier and NAS-Port-Type. Others describe the service to be delivered, such as Service-Type, Framed-Protocol, Framed-IP-Address, Framed-IP-Netmask, Framed-Routing, Framed-MTU, Framed-Compression and Filter-Id. The State attribute is used to carry information between an Access-Challenge and the following Access-Request, and the Reply-Message attribute carries a text string for display to the user. Proxy-State is added by a forwarding proxy when it forwards a request and removed when it forwards the response, which means the proxy has to re-sign the reply because Access-Accept and Access-Reject replies are authenticated on the entire packet contents.
sections.plainLanguage: Attributes are the name/value pairs inside the packet: who is calling, which line, the scrambled password, and the settings to apply if the answer is yes.

sections.title: Why UDP Rather Than TCP
sections.content:
The RFC explains why RADIUS uses UDP instead of TCP, on strictly technical grounds. First, if a request to a primary authentication server fails, a secondary server must be queried, so a copy of the request must be kept above the transport layer to allow for alternate transmission, which means retransmission timers are still required either way.

Second, the timing requirements of this protocol are significantly different from what TCP provides. At one extreme RADIUS does not require a responsive detection of lost data, because the user is willing to wait several seconds for the authentication to complete, and the generally aggressive TCP retransmission is not required, nor is the acknowledgement overhead of TCP. At the other extreme the user is not willing to wait several minutes, so the reliable delivery of TCP data two minutes later is not useful, and the faster use of an alternate server allows the user to gain access before giving up.

Third, the stateless nature of this protocol simplifies the use of UDP. Clients and servers come and go, systems are rebooted or power cycled independently, and this generally does not cause a problem, since with creative timeouts and detection of lost TCP connections, code can be written to handle anomalous events. UDP completely eliminates this special handling, because each client and server can open their UDP transport once and leave it open through all types of failure event on the network.

Fourth, UDP simplifies the server implementation. In the earliest implementations the server was single threaded, so a single request was received, processed and returned. That was found to be unmanageable where the back-end security mechanism took real time, since the request queue would fill and turn-around time increased beyond what users were willing to wait. The obvious solution was to make the server multi-threaded, which was simple with UDP: separate processes were spawned to serve each request and could respond directly to the client with a simple UDP packet to the original transport of the client. The RFC concedes the one penalty: with UDP, retransmission timers must be managed artificially.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication is one question and one answer, and the user will not wait for minutes but does not need instant failure detection either. UDP with its own timers fits that better than a connection-oriented transport.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security issues are the primary topic of this document, and its Security Considerations section, which follows the Examples, says that within or associated with each RADIUS server there is a database which associates user names with authentication information. It is not anticipated that a particular named user would be authenticated by multiple methods, because that would make the user vulnerable to attacks which negotiate the least secure method from among a set. Instead, for each named user there should be an indication of exactly one method used to authenticate that user name, and if a user needs different authentication methods under different circumstances then distinct user names SHOULD be employed.

Passwords and other secrets should be stored at the respective ends such that access to them is as limited as possible, and ideally the secrets should only be accessible to the process requiring access in order to perform the authentication. The secrets should be distributed with a mechanism that limits the number of entities that handle, and thus gain knowledge of, the secret, so that ideally no unauthorized person ever gains knowledge of them.

Two administrative notes in the body of the memo add to this. The shared secret SHOULD be at least as large and unguessable as a well-chosen password, and it is preferred that it be at least 16 octets, to ensure a sufficiently large range for protection against exhaustive search attacks. A RADIUS server SHOULD use the source IP address of the RADIUS UDP packet to decide which shared secret to use, so that RADIUS requests can be proxied.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the shared secret long and keep it to as few machines as possible, and do not let one user name be accepted by several different authentication methods, because an attacker would then pick the weakest one.

messages.label: ACCESS-REQUEST
messages.note: User-Name, a hidden password, and the NAS identity and port.

messages.label: ACCESS-ACCEPT
messages.note: The service type and the settings the NAS should apply.

messages.label: ACCESS-REJECT
messages.note: Sent instead when a condition is not met.

messages.note: Asks the user a question; the client answers with a new Access-Request.

fields.desc: Identifies the type of RADIUS packet.

fields.desc: Aids in matching requests and replies.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the packet in octets; minimum 20 and maximum 4096.

fields.name: Authenticator
fields.desc: A 16 octet random number in a request, and a one-way MD5 hash in a reply.

fields.name: Attributes
fields.desc: A variable number of Attribute-Length-Value triples.

items.label: Access-Request

items.desc: The request succeeded; carries the configuration to apply.

items.desc: The request failed; no other attributes are permitted.

items.label: Access-Challenge
items.desc: Asks the user to respond to a challenge.
